title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Texas Gulf Sulphur Co.
lead: After an earlier en banc decision established securities violations surrounding Texas Gulf Sulphur’s ore discovery, the parties returned to court over the company’s press release and appropriate remedies. The Second Circuit upheld the challenged rulings except cancellation of one stock option, which required a remedy hearing.

actors.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
actors.role: Federal regulator seeking enforcement and equitable relief.

actors.name: Texas Gulf Sulphur Company
actors.role: Mining company, abbreviated TGS, responsible for the disputed release.

actors.name: Clayton, Crawford, Holyk, Huntington, and Darke
actors.role: Individual defendants whose trading or remedies were at issue.

actors.role: Author of the unanimous appellate opinion.

proceedings: Following the 1968 en banc liability decision, Judge Bonsal decided remanded liability and remedies. The 1971 panel affirmed all challenged rulings except Kline’s option cancellation and remanded that remedy for a hearing.
limits: This account concerns the 1971 appeal, not a newly adjudicated discovery or landowner-disclosure claim. Paragraph pinpoints follow the preserved reproduction. Historical speech and securities-law formulations are not current-law certification.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A mineral discovery leads to securities litigation
sections.cue: The earlier appeal leaves remedies and corporate liability to the trial court.
paragraphs: Texas Gulf Sulphur Company, or TGS, discovered rich ore near Timmins, Ontario. The assigned account describes aerial detection of an electromagnetic anomaly, acquisition of nearby mineral rights and options, and insider stock purchases before public announcement. The Securities and Exchange Commission brought the securities enforcement action; this appeal did not adjudicate the separate landowner-disclosure dispute mentioned in the assignment.

The first trial found several defendants not liable under section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. In 1968 the Second Circuit sitting en banc reversed some liability determinations and remanded for remedies and an unresolved corporate-liability question. The parties had stipulated that remedies would await liability.

On remand, District Judge Bonsal enjoined individual defendants Clayton and Crawford, declined injunctions against TGS and several others, ordered surrender of specified trading profits, and canceled defendant Kline’s stock option. Defendant Darke’s repayment included profits earned by people he had tipped. O’Neill was subject to a default repayment order but did not appeal. The ensuing 1971 appeal therefore concerned those remand decisions, with the earlier liability rulings largely settled.

sources.pinpoint: Reproduced opinion ¶1 & nn.1–3; assigned printed p.509

sections.title: The company’s press release is found misleading
sections.cue: Shareholders’ reactions inform but do not decide the reasonable-investor question.
paragraphs: TGS’s April 12, 1964 press release tried to dispel rumors about exploratory drilling. The prior appeal left two questions for remand: whether the release misled a reasonable investor and whether lack of due diligence caused that result. Former shareholders testified that the release prompted them to sell. TGS objected that this was nonexpert opinion on the ultimate issue and presented witnesses who viewed the release as optimistic. The district court found it misleading but denied an injunction because future violation was not reasonably likely.

Judge Waterman, writing with Chief Judge Friendly and Judge Hays, upheld the testimony. The shareholders described their own reasons for selling, relevant evidence rather than an ultimate legal determination. Properly founded accounts of perception can contain subjective conclusions, particularly in a nonjury proceeding. Whether particular investors were reasonable affected weight and was explored on cross-examination. The trial judge’s careful evaluation of conflicting testimony was not clearly erroneous.

TGS also claimed that the due-diligence finding merely adopted the earlier appellate view. It offered no additional evidence on that point on remand, and agreement did not show absence of independent judgment. The panel rejected a First Amendment objection, reasoning in this historical opinion that a factual corporate release resembled registration statements and prospectuses rather than an exchange of ideas. The prior appeal had not foreclosed that constitutional argument.

sections.title: Prospective injunctions turn on the particular defendants
sections.cue: Past violations can remain adjudicated without an injunction.
paragraphs: Clayton and Crawford argued that injunctions singled them out unfairly and lacked a basis in likely repetition. Both had traded on inside information within twenty-four hours before public disclosure and had been found liable even under the first trial’s legal principles. That distinguished them from defendants whose liability depended on subsequent legal development. Their injunctions addressed future TGS transactions using undisclosed material information acquired through an insider relationship. The panel found no abuse of discretion. Clayton could not relitigate the execution timing of his purchase because the prior decision had settled it.

Conversely, TGS and defendants Fogarty, Mollison, and Stephens were not entitled to dismissal or erasure of their adjudicated violations merely because they were not enjoined. Past liability and a need for future restraints were distinct questions.

sections.title: The court upholds surrender of pre-disclosure gains
sections.cue: The remedy removes the benefit of wrongdoing without taking later appreciation.
paragraphs: Holyk, Huntington, Clayton, and Darke had to surrender profits accrued from their purchases through April 17, 1964, when the discovery was fully public. The funds would remain in interest-bearing escrow for five years under court supervision, with undistributed amounts then belonging to TGS. Private judgments arising from the same events would be paid from the fund to protect against double liability.

The appellants argued that section 21(e) authorized only injunctions and necessary ancillary relief and that surrender without direct compensation of injured sellers was an unlawful penalty. The panel distinguished district courts’ general equitable power under section 27 from the Commission’s authority to invoke it. Receivership and governmental-restitution analogies, statutory purposes, text, and legislative history supported appropriate remedial relief beyond prohibitory injunctions. The limitation was remedial relief rather than a penalty assessment.

The order removed pre-disclosure gains while preserving later appreciation. The stipulated April 17 average price was $40.375; by May 15 shares were $58.25. In effect, restitution moved acquisition to the date information became public. Darke’s liability for tippee profits created greater hardship, but omitting those gains would permit evasion through relatives, acquaintances, or reciprocal tips. TGS itself could suffer reputational and shareholder-relations injury. Sellers might have a superior equity, but that did not preclude conditional compensation of the company. The restitution order stood.

sections.title: One remedy was imposed without the promised opportunity to contest it
sections.cue: The remaining procedural objection does not undo the appeal.
paragraphs: The earlier en banc court had directed cancellation of Kline’s option even though remedies had not been briefed or argued under the stipulation. Judge Bonsal followed that clear direction without a hearing. The panel acknowledged the earlier mistake: authority to cancel an option did not eliminate Kline’s opportunity to contest whether that remedy was appropriate. It reversed cancellation and remanded for a hearing. Liability remained settled, but the borderline extent of Kline’s knowledge could bear on relief. The panel did not hold that the option must survive.

Crawford separately claimed a statutory and constitutional right to oral argument before at least a quorum of the en banc court. The panel treated section 46(c) as conferring institutional power and generally leaving hearing procedure to judicial discretion. Equal treatment of the parties did not require renewed oral argument as a matter of due process. The opinion expressly reserved the different question of dispensing with argument on an initial appeal.
The final judgment affirmed every challenged ruling except Kline’s option cancellation. No judge wrote separately.
